h1: Preparing for the IBD General Certificate in Brewing
title: IBD General Certificate: How to Prepare | Craft Beer School
desc: How to prepare for the IBD General Certificate in Brewing from India: what it covers, how to study, practise and plan your exam.
teaser: The General Certificate is the first rung of the IBD ladder. It rewards steady study more than brewing experience.
standfirst: The Institute of Brewing and Distilling's General Certificate in Brewing is a widely recognised entry qualification. Here is what it covers, how to prepare from India and what to do after you pass.
sections:
The Institute of Brewing and Distilling, usually called the IBD, is a professional body based in the UK with members around the world. Its qualifications are recognised by breweries in many countries. The General Certificate in Brewing is the entry level. It is designed for people who work in or around brewing and want a structured understanding of the whole process.

There are no formal entry requirements. Brewers, lab staff, packaging operators, engineers, sales people and career changers all sit it. Above it sit the Diploma in Brewing and the Master Brewer qualification, which go much deeper. Our guide to brewing certifications compares it with other options.

The syllabus follows beer from raw materials to the finished package. Broadly it includes:

  • Raw materials: water, malt, adjuncts, hops and yeast.
  • Brewhouse operations: milling, mashing, wort separation, boiling and wort cooling.
  • Fermentation and yeast management.
  • Beer processing: maturation, filtration and stabilisation.
  • Packaging: kegs, cans, bottles and pasteurisation.
  • Quality, hygiene, safety and environmental topics.

The IBD publishes the current syllabus, learning material, exam format, fees and exam windows on its website. These change from time to time, so check them before you plan your study. Do not rely on what a colleague remembers from a few years ago.

Most people with some brewing exposure need a few months of steady study. If you have never worked in a brewery, allow longer, because many terms will be new. A realistic plan for someone with a full-time job is a few hours a week over three to six months.

Spread the topics evenly. Candidates often spend weeks on the brewhouse because it feels familiar. Then they rush packaging and quality at the end. Those later sections carry real weight in the exam.

1. Read the official syllabus and turn each line into a question.
  2. Work through the learning material one section at a time.
  3. After each section, write a one page summary in your own words.
  4. Draw the process: a simple flow from malt intake to packaging, with temperatures and times.
  5. Practise with sample questions where the IBD provides them.
  6. Teach a section to someone else, even a friend outside brewing.

Learn numbers in context, not as a list. For example, a typical infusion mash rests around 62 to 68 °C, wort is boiled for roughly 60 to 90 minutes and lager fermentation usually runs around 8 to 13 °C. Knowing why each figure is what it is makes exam questions much easier than memorising them.

Indian candidates have one advantage and one challenge. The advantage is that many Indian breweries use rice and maize adjuncts, high gravity brewing and returnable glass, so topics that feel abstract elsewhere are visible on the floor here. If you work in a brewery, link each topic to something you can see.

The challenge is that the material is written for an international audience. Examples assume temperate climates and European raw materials. Note where Indian practice differs, such as water treatment for borewell supplies or the cold chain in summer heat, so you understand the principle rather than one country's habit. Our guide to brewing for India covers those differences.

Check the exam arrangements well in advance, including whether you sit at a centre or remotely, what identification you need and the time zone of the exam window. Read each question fully. Questions often test whether you understand cause and effect, so the obvious answer is not always correct. Manage your time and flag hard questions to return to.

If you do not pass first time, look at the feedback, focus on the weakest sections and sit again. Check the current resit rules on the IBD website.

Passing the General Certificate shows an employer that you understand the whole brewing process. It helps when applying for assistant brewer, QC or production roles. It is also a useful foundation for the Diploma in Brewing. The Diploma is a much bigger step and expects a solid grasp of brewing science, so many people take a few years of work and further study between the two. Our guide to a degree versus a short course covers the longer options.
faqs: Do I need brewing experience to take the IBD General Certificate?
No formal experience is required. Working in a brewery makes the material easier to understand, but career changers pass it regularly with good study.
Where can I find the current syllabus and exam dates?
On the Institute of Brewing and Distilling website. Check there for the current syllabus, format, fees and exam windows, because they change.
What comes after the General Certificate?
The IBD Diploma in Brewing and later the Master Brewer qualification. Many people work and study further for some years between levels.
